title: 🎙️ How I AI: OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance
text: 🎙️ How I AI: OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance Subscribe Sign in How I AI 🎙️ How I AI: OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance Your weekly listens from How I AI, part of the Lenny’s Podcast Network Lenny Rachitsky Nov 23, 2026 198 4 Share OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance | Ankit Maheshwari (Innovaccer) Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts Brought to you by: Parallel —Web search built for AI scale GiveDirectly —Send cash to the world’s poorest Ankit Maheshwari is the CTO of Innovaccer and the creator of a personal AI chief of staff he runs through OpenClaw on a Mac Mini. In this episode, he shows how his Jarvis handles work approvals, orders lunch, calls coworkers who miss Slack messages, books restaurants, and controls his smart home. He also explains how he uses soul files, specialist subagents, and strict guardrails to make the system trustworthy, and why he is testing local models against a $500 to $600 monthly Anthropic bill. Biggest takeaways: The best reason to stick with an agent platform is control, not habit. Ankit remains on OpenClaw because it can use his credentials, act on his behalf, and complete tasks without requesting permission at every step. That autonomy is an architectural advantage, not brand loyalty. Start with the bottleneck, not the grand vision. Ankit’s first automation was a cron job that runs every four hours and briefs him on every resume awaiting approval, including candidate pedigree and GitHub history. Once it worked, he began spotting similar bottlenecks throughout his day. Specialized agents outperform generalist ones once the workload becomes complex. Ankit’s master agent struggled to maintain the right persona across restaurant bookings and coworker check-ins. Moving voice calls to a dedicated agent improved consistency and clarified the split between orchestration and execution. Configuring soul files requires more work than integrations. The hardest part was defining each agent’s personality, boundaries, permissions, and routing logic through files such as soul.md. Getting those instructions right required more iteration than connecting the underlying tools. Guardrails should cover the worst case before it happens. OpenClaw once approved expiring travel requests while Ankit was in transit, using the same budget and customer-impact criteria he would have applied. The decisions were sound, but the experience exposed other actions, such as job-role approvals, that needed explicit limits. The model bill is worth optimizing before the system becomes indispensable. Jarvis costs Ankit roughly $500 to $600 per month on Opus 5.5. Early tests suggest a nearly free local model can handle summaries, email, cron checks, and call orchestration, while complex browser work still requires a frontier model. The “1% annoyance” rule is an effective way to discover automations. If a task is even slightly frustrating and repeats a few times, Ankit automates it. That approach led to agents for lunch ordering, unanswered Slack messages, home automation, and potentially even calling the elevator. A terminal-first approach can keep agent building surprisingly simple. Ankit set up OpenClaw by opening its terminal interface and speaking to it like a new employee. When coding was required, OpenClaw launched Claude Code and managed the implementation itself. Teach agents the messy details, then let them keep learning. Ankit’s lunch agent confirms his order at 9:30 a.m. and acts independently if he does not respond. After one correction about ordering curry without bread, it learned both when to add bread and when a meal already includes it.
